Our aim was to investigate the prevalence and degree of dyspareunia and level of satisfaction with the outcome of the perineal repair after a spontaneous second-degree tear compared to an episiotomy. Further, we aimed to identify risk factors for dyspareunia and dissatisfaction with the outcome. Material and methods This register-based cohort study included 5 328 primiparous women who sustained a spontaneous second-degree tear (n = 4 323) or an episiotomy (n = 1005) between 2014 and 2019 in Sweden. The primary outcomes were self-reported degree of dyspareunia and level of satisfaction with the outcome of the perineal repair at one year. Data were collected from national health and quality registers and online questionnaires at eight weeks and one year. Logistic regression was used and results are presented by Odds Ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) after adjustment for age, body mass index and mode of delivery. Results 30.0% of women with a spontaneous tear and 29.1% of women with an episiotomy reported mild or moderate dyspareunia, while 2.4% of women with a spontaneous tear compared to 3.8% of women with an episiotomy reported strong or unbearable dyspareunia (aOR 1.5; CI 0.9–2.4). 73.4% of women with a spontaneous tear and 67.1% with episiotomy were satisfied or very satisfied with their outcome, while 6.7% with an episiotomy compared to 3.7% with a spontaneous tear were dissatisfied (aOR 1.8; CI 1.2–2.6). Postpartum infection, scar dehiscence, re-suturing and perineal pain at eight weeks were risk factors for dyspareunia and dissatisfaction at one year. Conclusions Approximately one-third of women with either a spontaneous tear or an episiotomy reported mild or moderate dyspareunia at one year, while strong or unbearable pain was uncommon in both groups. The majority of women were satisfied or very satisfied with the outcome although episiotomy more often predicted dissatisfaction. Perineal tears are divided into first-degree which includes the vaginal mucosa or skin, second-degree which also involves the perineal muscles, and third- and fourth-degree which include in addition the anal sphincter [1]. Sexual function is important for quality of life and complaints such as dyspareunia and impaired sexual satisfaction are common among women during the first year postpartum [5–9]. Instrumental delivery, perineal tears, and episiotomies have been suggested as negatively impacting sexual function, although studies are small and results sometimes conflicting [7, 10]. Several studies have focused on length of time until resumed sexual intercourse and report that perineal trauma is associated with a delayed resumption of vaginal intercourse at six months after childbirth [11]. Dyspareunia is a complaint of persistent or recurrent pain or discomfort associated with attempted or completed vaginal penetration [12]. Postpartum dyspareunia is common, with frequencies varying between 20–40% at six months [5–9] and women with a second-degree tear are 80% more likely to report dyspareunia compared to women with an intact perineum [6]. The Perineal Study in Norway that included 561 respondents did not find that episiotomy compared to spontaneous second-degree tear was a risk factor for dyspareunia, however the numbers were small; only 8% had a spontaneous second-degree tear and 21% an episiotomy, while the rest had either intact perineum, first- or third-degree tears [13]. In contrast, the recent meta-analysis by Cattani et al. that included studies with sample size between 108 and 832 women, and a range of follow-up between five and 15 months, found that episiotomy compared with spontaneous tear was associated with dyspareunia [10]. Roman et al. highlighted in their recent qualitative meta-synthesis the importance of including the woman’s experience when conducting research on perineal tears [14]. fetched_contents.text: Network meta-analysis of episiotomy approaches: comparing routine, restrictive, and non-episiotomy strategies and their effects on maternal and neonatal outcomes in primiparous patients Abstract Background Episiotomy, although occasionally required during labor, can result in postpartum discomfort, perineal trauma, and delayed healing. This study offers a comprehensive comparison of the safety and effectiveness of routine, restrictive, and non-episiotomy approaches on maternal and neonatal outcomes. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane. We included randomized clinical trials (RCTs), comparing routine, restrictive, and non-episiotomy approaches in primiparous pregnant women. We excluded non-randomized trials, conference abstracts, and observational studies. The Cochrane ROB tool 2 was employed to appraise the selected RCTs. We conducted our analysis using the “netmeta” package of RStudio software (v.4.3.0). Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR), while continuous outcomes were pooled as the mean differences (MD). We used the random effect model for all outcomes. Results Sixteen studies, involving 10,738 patients, were included in the network meta-analysis. The findings revealed that the non-episiotomy group had a significantly higher risk of experiencing 1st-degree perineal tear compared to the routine episiotomy group (RR = 4.69, 95% CI [2.04; 10.74], P > 0.01). Similarly, the restrictive episiotomy group showed a significantly higher risk compared to the routine group (RR = 3.88, 95% CI [1.63; 9.26], P > 0.01). However, there were no significant differences observed between the routine, restrictive, and non-episiotomy groups regarding the duration of the 2nd stage of labor, postpartum perineal pain, and the occurrence of 2nd-, 3rd-, and 4th-degree perineal tears. Conclusion In conclusion, non-episiotomy approaches prove superior, with lower risks of complications compared to routine episiotomy. While restrictive episiotomy performs better than routine, it falls short of non-episiotomy methods. Therefore, non-episiotomy strategies are preferred, followed by restrictive episiotomy, with routine episiotomy being the least favorable. However, individual patient factors should guide treatment decisions, and further research is necessary to refine clinical practices. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12978-025-02132-9. Keywords: Episiotomy, Perineal trauma, Post-partum morbidities Introduction The practice of episiotomy—a surgical incision to widen the birth canal—dates back to 1742 when Sir Fielding Ould first introduced it to minimize maternal trauma [1]. Despite its initial adoption without robust scientific evidence, episiotomy gained widespread acceptance in the 20th century following recommendations from leading obstetricians like Gabbe and DeLee [2, 3]. Consequently, its routine use led to a sharp rise in episiotomy rates, particularly in hospital-based deliveries, increasing from 5% in 1900 to nearly 80% by 1950 [4]. Currently, episiotomies are performed in one in three vaginal deliveries, with rates 8.8 times higher in primiparous than multiparous women [5]. Despite the WHO’s 1996 recommendation to limit episiotomies to 10% of vaginal deliveries, global rates vary significantly, ranging from 8% in the Netherlands to 25% in the US, with Taiwan reaching 100% [6]. However, rising complications have prompted a shift toward a more conservative approach [7]. Midline and mediolateral episiotomies differ mainly in anatomical direction, incision angle, and the tissue planes they involve. Midline episiotomy is described as a vertical incision made in the midline of the perineum from the posterior fourchette toward the anus, with the incision commonly directed straight downward or slightly angled, though the exact angle varies by source [N1-R2][N1-R5]. StatPearls and other sources also state that the incision begins at the midline of the posterior fourchette and is directed laterally and downward at a minimum angle of 60 degrees [N1-R1][N5-F2]. In contrast, mediolateral episiotomy starts at the midline but is directed downward and outward at an angle of 45° to 60° toward the ischial tuberosities or the direction of the anus [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. GLOWM similarly notes that mediolateral episiotomy extends in the mediolateral direction after the initial incision in the fourchette and vagina [N2-R2].

On anatomical direction and incision angle, midline episiotomy is more strictly central and can be described as a straight or near-vertical incision, while mediolateral is clearly angled outward from the midline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R1]. The evidence is not uniform on exact angle ranges, but the consensus across sources is that mediolateral episiotomy is deliberately angled outward, often between 45° and 60°, while midline is either straight or angled less dramatically [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. One source also notes that midline episiotomies are more commonly performed in the United States, whereas mediolateral episiotomies are more common in other settings, which may reflect regional practice patterns rather than a universal technique difference [N2-R5].

Regarding incision depth and lateral spread, the evidence is more suggestive than fully detailed. Midline episiotomy is associated with a greater risk of deep perineal tears than mediolateral episiotomy, as one study found 14.8% deep perineal tears with midline compared to 7% with mediolateral [N4-R1]. This suggests that midline incisions may extend deeper into the perineal tissue plane, potentially reaching the deep perineal space, whereas mediolateral incisions are more superficially angled outward and may avoid this deeper plane [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Mediolateral episiotomy can also be extended to incise the levator ani, which may increase lateral spread but also provide more room during delivery [N4-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not quantify lateral spread in millimeters or provide precise depth measurements, so this should be treated as a qualitative distinction rather than a precise metric [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1].

Tissue planes and structures involved are also distinct. Midline episiotomy typically involves the perineal skin and mucosa, with the incision often extending into the vaginal canal and, in some descriptions, the rectum [N1-R1][N4-R5]. Mediolateral episiotomy begins in the soft tissues of the fourchette and vagina, then incises the perineum, and may extend into the levator ani if the incision is extended [N2-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that midline episiotomy can involve deeper perineal structures, such as the deep perineal fascia and muscles, which explains why it is associated with higher rates of deep perineal tears [N4-R1]. Overall, midline is more central and can extend deeper, while mediolateral is more lateral and may engage the levator ani [N4-R1][N4-R3].

In summary, the surgical-technique difference is clearest in direction and angle: midline is straight or minimally angled, while mediolateral is outwardly angled; depth is implied to be greater for midline; and tissue involvement differs by whether the incision reaches the levator ani or deep perineal structures [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3].

The methodological context for comparing episiotomy types is important because the evidence base is heterogeneous and study quality varies. The network meta-analysis of episiotomy approaches reports that most studies had an unclear risk of bias in terms of selection of reported results, with only four studies being low risk [N5-R1]. Another systematic review and meta-analysis of mediolateral/lateral episiotomy with operative vaginal delivery also found that the quality of all evidence was downgraded to “very low” because of the critical risk of bias across many studies [N5-R2]. This means that the conclusions should be interpreted cautiously and that many findings may be overestimated or inconsistent [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The same network meta-analysis also notes that results were interpreted in conjunction with risk of bias assessments and GRADE certainty ratings, which reinforces the importance of quality-adjusted interpretation [N5-R3].

Study design limitations affect comparison of episiotomy types in several ways. First, the evidence includes randomized clinical trials (RCTs) as well as observational studies, which differ substantially in validity [N5-R1]. The network meta-analysis explicitly excluded non-randomized trials, conference abstracts, and observational studies, but the broader literature still contains many observational studies, cohort studies, and register-based studies that may not control for confounding as well as RCTs [N5-F2]. Second, the evidence is heterogeneous in outcome measurement: some studies report dyspareunia, others report infection, hematoma, healing complications, and severe perineal trauma, and the measurement instruments and definitions can differ across trials [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3]. Third, follow-up varies widely, with some studies following women at 8 weeks, 6 months, or 1 year, and the provided evidence also includes a register-based cohort study with data collected at eight weeks and one year [N3-F1]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to combine findings directly and reduces confidence in pooled comparisons [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

Heterogeneity in outcome measurement and follow-up further complicates interpretation. The meta-analysis on dyspareunia after spontaneous second-degree tear versus episiotomy shows that the study design and follow-up period influence the results: a cohort study at one year found 30% mild/moderate dyspareunia in spontaneous tears and 29.1% in episiotomies, while a meta-analysis of 1210 women from five studies found that episiotomy more often experienced dyspareunia [N3-R1][N3-F1]. The cohort study also found that postpartum infection, scar dehiscence, re-suturing, and perineal pain at eight weeks were risk factors for dyspareunia at one year [N3-F1]. Similarly, the network meta-analysis on episiotomy approaches found no significant differences between routine, restrictive, and non-episiotomy groups for postpartum perineal pain and 2nd-, 3rd-, and 4th-degree tears, but it also notes that non-episiotomy strategies were superior overall [N5-F2]. This shows that some conclusions can be robust when outcomes are consistent and follow-up is standardized, while others remain speculative when evidence is sparse or heterogeneous [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Which conclusions are robust versus speculative? Robust conclusions are those supported by multiple sources and careful quality assessment. The evidence that episiotomy is associated with perineal pain, hematoma, infection, and dyspareunia is recurrent across multiple sources, including the network meta-analysis and the register-based cohort study [N5-F2][N3-F1]. The network meta-analysis concludes that non-episiotomy approaches are preferred, followed by restrictive episiotomy, with routine episiotomy being least favorable, but it also emphasizes that further research is needed to refine clinical practices [N5-F2]. Similarly, the dyspareunia evidence suggests episiotomy is more often associated with dyspareunia than spontaneous tear, but the exact magnitude differs by study and follow-up [N3-F1][N3-R1]. In short, the robust conclusions are about association and relative risk, while broader recommendations or definitive superiority claims are speculative unless supported by higher-quality, more homogeneous evidence [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N3-F1].

### Differences in deep perineal tears and surgical injury risk
Midline episiotomy is associated with a higher rate of deep perineal tears than mediolateral episiotomy [N4-R1]. Mediolateral episiotomy is described as an incision that can be extended to incise the levator ani, which may provide more room for delivery and potentially reduce the risk of deep perineal tears [N4-R3]. The evidence does not show that mediolateral episiotomy reduces all complications; it only clearly identifies a lower rate of deep perineal tears [N4-R1][N4-R3].

### Whether mediolateral episiotomy reduces complications or increases them
The evidence supports a cautious conclusion: **mediolateral episiotomy may reduce the risk of deep perineal tears compared to midline**, but it does not show that it reduces all complications [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The broader safety context in the network meta-analysis indicates that non-episiotomy approaches are preferred overall, and that routine episiotomy is associated with lower safety compared to restrictive or non-episiotomy strategies [N5-F2]. This means that mediolateral episiotomy may be better than midline for some complications, but its overall complication profile is best assessed in the context of the broader evidence on episiotomy versus non-episiotomy strategies [N4-R1][N5-F2].

---

## 4. Methodological context and interpretation

### Study design limitations affecting comparison of episiotomy types
The methodological context is important because the evidence base is heterogeneous and study quality varies. The network meta-analysis reports that most studies had an unclear risk of bias in terms of selection of reported results, with only four studies being low risk [N5-R1]. Another systematic review and meta-analysis of mediolateral/lateral episiotomy with operative vaginal delivery found that the quality of all evidence was downgraded to “very low” because of the critical risk of bias across many studies [N5-R2]. This means that conclusions should be interpreted cautiously, and many findings may be overestimated or inconsistent [N5-R1][N5-R2].

### Heterogeneity in outcome measurement and follow-up
Outcome measurement differs across studies. Some studies report dyspareunia, others report infection, hematoma, healing complications, and severe perineal trauma, and the measurement instruments and definitions can differ across trials [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3]. Follow-up also varies widely, with some studies following women at 8 weeks, 6 months, or 1 year, and the provided evidence includes a register-based cohort study with data collected at eight weeks and one year [N3-F1]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to combine findings directly and reduces confidence in pooled comparisons [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

### Which conclusions are robust versus speculative
Robust conclusions are those supported by multiple sources and careful quality assessment. The evidence that episiotomy is associated with perineal pain, hematoma, infection, and dyspareunia is recurrent across multiple sources [N5-F2][N3-F1]. The evidence that midline episiotomy is associated with a greater rate of deep perineal tears than mediolateral episiotomy is also specific and comes from a direct comparative study [N4-R1]. However, conclusions about which type is “better overall” are more speculative because the evidence is mixed and heterogeneous [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

In short, the robust conclusions are about association and relative risk, while broader recommendations or definitive superiority claims are speculative unless supported by higher-quality, more homogeneous evidence [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N3-F1].

---

## 5. Bottom line

- **Surgical technique**: midline is central and straight or minimally angled; mediolateral is outwardly angled at 45°–60° [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R5].
- **Incision depth and spread**: midline may extend deeper and is associated with more deep perineal tears; mediolateral may extend into the levator ani and is associated with fewer deep perineal tears [N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Tissue involvement**: midline involves deeper perineal structures; mediolateral may engage the levator ani [N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Dyspareunia**: episiotomy is associated with increased dyspareunia risk, but the magnitude and long-term course depend on comparator, follow-up, and study design [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1].
- **Complications**: midline is associated with more deep perineal tears; mediolateral may reduce this risk, but does not eliminate all complications [N4-R1][N5-F2].
- **Methodological context**: the evidence is heterogeneous, with many studies having unclear or very low risk of bias, so conclusions should be cautious [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Overall, midline and mediolateral episiotomies differ mainly in direction and depth of incision, and the choice between them should weigh surgical advantage against postpartum risk, with the evidence suggesting that mediolateral may reduce some complications while episiotomy remains associated with dyspareunia and healing problems [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1][N5-F2][N3-F1].

Branch report on surgical technique differences

Midline and mediolateral episiotomies differ mainly in anatomical direction, incision angle, and the tissue planes they involve. Midline episiotomy is described as a vertical incision made in the midline of the perineum from the posterior fourchette toward the anus, with the incision commonly directed straight downward or slightly angled, though the exact angle varies by source [N1-R2][N1-R5]. StatPearls and other sources also state that the incision begins at the midline of the posterior fourchette and is directed laterally and downward at a minimum angle of 60 degrees [N1-R1][N5-F2]. In contrast, mediolateral episiotomy starts at the midline but is directed downward and outward at an angle of 45° to 60° toward the ischial tuberosities or the direction of the anus [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. GLOWM similarly notes that mediolateral episiotomy extends in the mediolateral direction after the initial incision in the fourchette and vagina [N2-R2].

On anatomical direction and incision angle, midline episiotomy is more strictly central and can be described as a straight or near-vertical incision, while mediolateral is clearly angled outward from the midline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R1]. The evidence is not uniform on exact angle ranges, but the consensus across sources is that mediolateral episiotomy is deliberately angled outward, often between 45° and 60°, while midline is either straight or angled less dramatically [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. One source also notes that midline episiotomies are more commonly performed in the United States, whereas mediolateral episiotomies are more common in other settings, which may reflect regional practice patterns rather than a universal technique difference [N2-R5].

Regarding incision depth and lateral spread, the evidence is more suggestive than fully detailed. Midline episiotomy is associated with a greater risk of deep perineal tears than mediolateral episiotomy, as one study found 14.8% deep perineal tears with midline compared to 7% with mediolateral [N4-R1]. This suggests that midline incisions may extend deeper into the perineal tissue plane, potentially reaching the deep perineal space, whereas mediolateral incisions are more superficially angled outward and may avoid this deeper plane [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Mediolateral episiotomy can also be extended to incise the levator ani, which may increase lateral spread but also provide more room during delivery [N4-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not quantify lateral spread in millimeters or provide precise depth measurements, so this should be treated as a qualitative distinction rather than a precise metric [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1].

Tissue planes and structures involved are also distinct. Midline episiotomy typically involves the perineal skin and mucosa, with the incision often extending into the vaginal canal and, in some descriptions, the rectum [N1-R1][N4-R5]. Mediolateral episiotomy begins in the soft tissues of the fourchette and vagina, then incises the perineum, and may extend into the levator ani if the incision is extended [N2-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that midline episiotomy can involve deeper perineal structures, such as the deep perineal fascia and muscles, which explains why it is associated with higher rates of deep perineal tears [N4-R1]. Overall, midline is more central and can extend deeper, while mediolateral is more lateral and may engage the levator ani [N4-R1][N4-R3].

In summary, the surgical-technique difference is clearest in direction and angle: midline is straight or minimally angled, while mediolateral is outwardly angled; depth is implied to be greater for midline; and tissue involvement differs by whether the incision reaches the levator ani or deep perineal structures [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3].

Study design limitations affect comparison of episiotomy types in several ways. The evidence on dyspareunia after episiotomy is mixed but suggests a consistent association overall. A register-based cohort study found that 30.0% of women with a spontaneous second-degree tear and 29.1% with episiotomy reported mild or moderate dyspareunia at one year, while 2.4% of spontaneous-tear women and 3.8% of episiotomy women reported strong or unbearable dyspareunia [N3-F1]. A meta-analysis of 1210 women from five studies also reported that episiotomy more often experienced dyspareunia [N3-R1]. In contrast, a systematic review and meta-analysis of continuous versus interrupted perineal repair found no statistically significant difference in postpartum dyspareunia between the two groups [N3-R2]. This discrepancy shows that dyspareunia is not uniformly higher after episiotomy; instead, the risk may depend on the comparator, follow-up, and study design [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1].

The overall magnitude of dyspareunia risk is therefore not straightforward. The register-based study shows that episiotomy is associated with a small but clinically meaningful excess of dyspareunia: 3.8% strong or unbearable dyspareunia after episiotomy versus 2.4% after spontaneous tear [N3-F1]. The meta-analysis of 1210 women similarly supports a higher risk of dyspareunia after episiotomy, though it does not provide a precise relative risk estimate in the excerpt provided [N3-R1]. The absence of a significant difference in the continuous versus interrupted repair meta-analysis suggests that dyspareunia may not always be uniquely attributable to episiotomy itself, but rather to other perineal trauma or repair characteristics [N3-R2]. Therefore, the most defensible conclusion is that episiotomy is associated with increased dyspareunia risk compared to some comparators, but not universally above all comparators [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1].

Evidence also suggests differences in persistence or severity over time. The register-based cohort study followed women at eight weeks and one year and found that dyspareunia persisted into the medium term, with 30% reporting mild/moderate dyspareunia at one year [N3-F1]. It also found that postpartum infection, scar dehiscence, re-suturing, and perineal pain at eight weeks were risk factors for dyspareunia at one year [N3-F1]. This indicates that dyspareunia may not resolve quickly and may persist or recur depending on healing complications. The meta-analysis of 1210 women and the cohort study both suggest that dyspareunia can be persistent, but the exact trajectory is not fully quantified in the available evidence [N3-R1][N3-F1]. The cohort study also found that dissatisfaction was more common after episiotomy than after spontaneous tear, which implies that dyspareunia may be accompanied by dissatisfaction and may not simply be a transient or mild issue [N3-F1].

Study design affects dyspareunia conclusions in three key ways. First, observational and register-based studies may have confounding because they cannot fully control for indications for episiotomy, perineal trauma severity, or postpartum care [N3-F1][N5-R1]. Second, outcome measurement differs: some studies use self-reported dyspareunia, while others use pain scales, satisfaction, or other endpoints [N3-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3]. Third, follow-up differs, with some studies following women at 8 weeks, 6 months, or 1 year, which can change the apparent magnitude and persistence of dyspareunia [N3-F1][N5-R3]. The network meta-analysis notes that results were interpreted in conjunction with risk of bias assessments and GRADE certainty ratings, which further supports the idea that conclusions should be cautiously interpreted [N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports a real but heterogeneous association between episiotomy and dyspareunia, with the strongest conclusions coming from register-based and meta-analytic evidence, but the exact magnitude and long-term course remain dependent on study design [N3-F1][N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

### Heterogeneity in outcome measurement and follow-up
Outcome measurement differs across studies. Some studies report dyspareunia, others report infection, hematoma, healing complications, and severe perineal trauma, and the measurement instruments and definitions can differ across trials [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3]. Follow-up also varies widely, with some studies following women at 8 weeks, 6 months, or 1 year, and the provided evidence includes a register-based cohort study with data collected at eight weeks and one year [N3-F1]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to combine findings directly and reduces confidence in pooled comparisons [N3-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

### Which conclusions are robust versus speculative
Robust conclusions are those supported by multiple sources and careful quality assessment. The evidence that episiotomy is associated with perineal pain, hematoma, infection, and dyspareunia is recurrent across multiple sources [N5-F2][N3-F1]. The evidence that midline episiotomy is associated with a greater rate of deep perineal tears than mediolateral episiotomy is also specific and comes from a direct comparative study [N4-R1]. However, conclusions about which type is “better overall” are more speculative because the evidence is mixed and heterogeneous [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

In short, the robust conclusions are about association and relative risk, while broader recommendations or definitive superiority claims are speculative unless supported by higher-quality, more homogeneous evidence [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N3-F1].

---

## 5. Bottom line

- **Surgical technique**: midline is central and straight or minimally angled; mediolateral is outwardly angled at 45°–60° [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R5].
- **Incision depth and spread**: midline may extend deeper and is associated with more deep perineal tears; mediolateral may extend into the levator ani and is associated with fewer deep perineal tears [N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Tissue involvement**: midline involves deeper perineal structures; mediolateral may engage the levator ani [N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Dyspareunia**: episiotomy is associated with increased dyspareunia risk, but the magnitude and long-term course depend on comparator, follow-up, and study design [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1].
- **Complications**: midline is associated with more deep perineal tears; mediolateral may reduce this risk, but does not eliminate all complications [N4-R1][N5-F2].
- **Methodological context**: the evidence is heterogeneous, with many studies having unclear or very low risk of bias, so conclusions should be cautious [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Overall, midline and mediolateral episiotomies differ mainly in direction and depth of incision, and the choice between them should weigh surgical advantage against postpartum risk, with the evidence suggesting that mediolateral may reduce some complications while episiotomy remains associated with dyspareunia and healing problems [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-R1][N5-F2][N3-F1].
